description:
I think this is an ancient Maya earth clock- let me tell you why.

The ancient Mayans had a two clock system comprised of two counts known as Tzolk’in (sacred) & Haad (solar) that worked in unison to project the - date known as the  “Calendar Round,” which is the coincidental time where both of the clocks converge at single point. 
1. The center dial sits on a solid crystal shaft with a mushroom head and spins freely until it hits a certain portion that has a magnetic catch in it. It certainly would be affected my it’s position in relation to the Earth’s magnet field. I believe this represents the Haad portion.
2. The small outer dial is completely removable and free spinning. I believe this part is activated by frequency, possibly in conjunction with specific types of UV light produced only on certain days from certain angles of the sun, such as high noon or the last hour setting sunlight on the summer or winter solstice. I believe this represents the Haab portion of the Mayan clock. 
3. The ratios of both dials seemed to correlate with the respective sizes of the calendars I believe they represent, with the larger dial representing Haab’s 365 days and the smaller corresponding to Tzolk’in’s 260 days.
4. Both dials plainly look like time pieces and contain all the parts of traditional clockwork.
5. The pointed arrow on the right is completely fixed in place and I could not move whatsoever. I tried several times, but gave up for fear of breaking it. There is no concrete or glue visible from any angle and I cannot tell how it is held in place but I believe that, if correctly activated, will to point to star system or astronomic feature to convey to a certain point in time, possibly calculated via precessional cycles and contains an inscription of the sun, which is a reference to precession and something common to many ancient artifacts of the time. The shape of the arrow obviously plainly looks like an indicator of some kind and I believe this represents the Mayan Calendar Round date.
These are my assumptions based off a lifetime of study.
